opus-5.5.text:
I think the way we write software is going to shift from telling the computer *how* to do something toward telling it precisely *what* we want. Right now, most programming is imperative — you spell out every step, and then you write tests that sample a handful of cases and hope they cover the important behavior. But tests are only spot checks. They can show the presence of bugs, not their absence.

Program specification flips that. You write down, in a formal language, the properties your program must satisfy — this function always returns a sorted list, this transaction never double-spends, this controller never enters an unsafe state. And then the implementation, whether it's written by a human or increasingly by an AI model, comes with a machine-checkable proof that it actually meets that spec. The proof checker, something like Lean, doesn't care who wrote the code. It either verifies or it doesn't.

Why does this matter now? Because AI is about to generate an enormous amount of code — far more than humans can review line by line. If we keep relying on human code review as the trust layer, that becomes the bottleneck, and frankly a dangerous one. Verification gives us a scalable trust layer. The human's job moves up a level: you think carefully about intent, you write or review the spec, and you let the AI do the grinding work of producing both the code and the proof.

Historically, formal verification was considered too expensive — projects like seL4 or CompCert took years of expert effort. What's changing is that the same reasoning capabilities we're building for mathematical proof transfer directly to proving properties of programs. Code is math, in a very real sense. So I see a future where verified code is the default for anything critical — infrastructure, finance, aerospace, medical devices — and eventually it trickles down to everyday software as the cost approaches zero.

The hard, interesting problem left for humans is the spec itself. Getting the spec right is really about understanding what you want, and that's a deeply human question. So I'd say the programmer of the future looks a bit more like a mathematician or a careful lawyer — someone who states precisely what should be true — with AI as the tireless collaborator that makes it so, and proves it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important shift is that the unit of programming stops being code and becomes intent. Today, when you write software, you're doing two jobs at once: deciding what the system should do, and figuring out how to make a machine do it. Those have always been tangled together, and that tangling is where most bugs live. You think you specified one thing, you actually wrote another, and you don't find out until something breaks in production.

Program specification pulls those apart. You state precisely what you want, in a form that can be checked, and the implementation becomes something that can be generated, verified, and regenerated. With language models now able to write enormous amounts of code very quickly, the bottleneck is no longer producing code. The bottleneck is knowing whether the code is right. And the only honest answer to "is it right" is "right relative to what?" That "what" is the specification.

So I imagine a future where a developer's day looks less like typing and more like thinking carefully about properties. What invariants should hold? What should never happen? What does correctness mean for this system? You write that down, the model proposes an implementation, and a verifier either proves it meets the spec or shows you exactly where it diverges. The loop is spec, generate, verify, refine. When verification fails, you learn something, either about the implementation or about your own understanding, and both are valuable.

This is where the connection to mathematics becomes very direct for me. A specification is essentially a theorem statement, and a verified program is a proof that the theorem holds. Formal systems like Lean have shown that this is practical, not just theoretical. And once the proof is machine-checked, trust stops depending on how carefully some human reviewed the code. It depends on the specification itself, which is much smaller, much more readable, and much easier to reason about.

I don't think this eliminates programmers. It elevates them. Writing a good specification is hard. It requires understanding the domain deeply and being honest about edge cases. That's exactly the skill that experienced engineers already have but that gets buried under boilerplate. In this future, that skill becomes the whole job.

And there's a broader point. As we hand more and more consequential systems to AI, "it seemed to work when we tested it" is not going to be good enough. Specification gives us a way to say what we actually mean and to hold the machine to it. I think that's the only path to software we can genuinely trust at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think coding will increasingly become about specifying what you want a program to do, rather than spelling out every step of how it should do it. You describe the desired behavior, the constraints, and what counts as a correct result, and an AI system helps produce the implementation.

But the specification is really the hard part. We often discover what we actually want while building something. So I imagine an interactive process: the system asks clarifying questions, shows you examples, and points out cases where your requirements conflict or leave something undefined. You refine the specification together.

What excites me is connecting that process to verification. If we can express important properties precisely, we can check whether the generated code satisfies them. Of course, proving that code meets a specification doesn’t prove that the specification captures your intent. Human judgment still matters enormously. The shift is that more of our effort goes toward deciding what should be built and articulating why it’s correct.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll spend less time telling computers exactly how to do something and more time specifying what we want the result to satisfy. Instead of writing every step of an implementation, you could describe the behavior, the constraints, and the properties that should always hold, and have a system generate code that meets that specification.

But the hard part doesn’t disappear. Specifications can be incomplete or ambiguous. So I imagine this as an interactive process: the system asks clarifying questions, shows you examples and counterexamples, and helps you refine what you actually mean. Where we can, we should also verify that the resulting program satisfies those properties, rather than simply trusting code that looks plausible.

That changes the programmer’s role. Understanding the problem, choosing the right abstractions, and expressing intent precisely become even more important. The exciting possibility is making software easier to create while also giving us stronger reasons to believe it does what we intended.
